title: Fuel and Oil Systems — Types, Contamination, and Engine Cooling

questions.text: A low-wing aircraft (Piper Cherokee) pilot is completing the before-takeoff checklist. The checklist calls for the electric fuel boost pump to be turned ON before takeoff. The pilot asks: 'The engine is already running fine on the engine-driven pump — why do I need the boost pump on for takeoff?'

options.label: A
options.text: The boost pump is required by FAA regulation for all low-wing aircraft departures — 14 CFR 91.205 mandates an electric fuel pump ON for all takeoff and landing operations regardless of aircraft configuration

options.label: B
options.text: Low-wing aircraft require the boost pump during takeoff to overcome the upward pressure differential — the fuel must travel from wing tanks below the engine upward against gravity; at low throttle settings on initial climb, the engine-driven pump produces insufficient pressure to lift fuel against gravity; the boost pump supplements at low power

options.label: C
options.text: The boost pump is on for engine failure contingency — if the engine-driven fuel pump fails during the most critical phase of flight (takeoff), the electric boost pump provides immediate backup fuel flow without requiring the pilot to diagnose and switch systems; having the boost pump already ON means fuel flow continues uninterrupted if the engine-driven pump fails at the worst possible moment

options.label: D
options.text: The boost pump reduces vapor lock in hot-summer operations — avgas at high temperature vaporizes in fuel lines if pressure is insufficient; the boost pump adds line pressure to prevent vapor from forming in the fuel lines during the high-power takeoff phase

questions.explanation: The electric fuel boost pump requirement for low-wing aircraft during takeoff and landing is a contingency measure — not a normal flow requirement. In normal operation, the engine-driven fuel pump provides adequate fuel pressure for all flight phases. The boost pump is selected ON before takeoff for a specific reason: engine failure contingency. If the engine-driven pump fails during the takeoff roll or initial climb (the most critical phases with minimum altitude and minimum options), the electric pump needs to be ALREADY running and providing flow. If the pilot had to diagnose 'engine-driven pump failure' then switch the boost pump ON during the emergency, precious seconds would be lost at minimum altitude. Having the boost pump already on provides seamless fuel flow continuity if the primary pump fails. This is the same logic as having landing gear down and locked for landing — the backup is pre-positioned. The 'required for landing' answer incorrectly claims the engine-driven pump cannot supply fuel upward — engine-driven pumps are fully capable of supplying fuel regardless of tank-to-engine geometry; they are positive displacement pumps that push fuel regardless of gravity. The 'vapor lock prevention' answer (vapor lock prevention) is a legitimate secondary benefit but not the primary purpose.

questions.text: After reaching cruise altitude at 9,500 feet, a pilot reduces power from climb to cruise settings by pulling the throttle rapidly to idle, then resetting to cruise power. The CHT drops from 380°F to 220°F in approximately 90 seconds. What is the concern and long-term consequence?

options.label: A
options.text: No concern — rapid CHT reduction is desirable for engine longevity; cooling aluminum cylinders quickly prevents heat soak into the cylinder head material; modern aviation engines are designed for rapid temperature cycling and the 160°F drop is within normal operating parameters

options.label: B
options.text: The concern is oil thinning — rapid temperature drop causes engine oil to temporarily increase viscosity at the contact points between piston rings and cylinder walls; this increased viscosity prevents proper ring sealing for 3-5 minutes after the rapid cooldown; any increased power application in this window risks blowby

options.label: C
options.text: Shock cooling — the rapid CHT drop of 160°F in 90 seconds (approximately 107°F per minute, well above the 50°F/minute maximum guideline) subjects the aluminum cylinder heads to thermal stress from differential contraction with the steel cylinder barrels; over repeated occurrences, this causes micro-cracking of the cylinder head, particularly around the exhaust valve seats; repair requires cylinder head replacement or comprehensive engine teardown

options.label: D
options.text: Concern is minimal — the 50°F per minute guideline is a manufacturer recommendation, not an airworthiness standard; a single 90-second shock cooling event will not cause measurable cylinder damage; the concern only applies to chronic pattern of repeated shock cooling events over hundreds of hours

questions.explanation: Shock cooling is a documented engine damage mechanism specific to air-cooled aluminum aircraft engines. The physics: (1) Aluminum cylinder heads and steel attachment bolts/barrels have different coefficients of thermal expansion. (2) Rapid cooling causes aluminum to contract faster than steel. (3) The differential contraction creates stress at the interface between aluminum and steel components — specifically around the exhaust valve seats, cylinder head/barrel interface, and mounting bosses. (4) Repeated thermal stress cycles create fatigue micro-cracks. (5) Cracks allow combustion gases to bypass the exhaust valve seat → reduced compression, rough running, eventually through-crack and catastrophic loss. The 50°F/minute maximum CHT decrease rate is the widely used industry guideline from engine manufacturers (Continental, Lycoming). A 107°F/minute drop (as in this scenario) is more than double the guideline. Correct technique: reduce power gradually in cruise descents — typically 100-200 RPM or 1-2 in. Hg per minute, monitoring CHT to keep the rate of decrease below 50°F/minute. The 'concern is minimal' answer invents a 'single event is fine' exception that is inconsistent with metallurgical fatigue principles — damage is cumulative.

questions.text: During a cross-country cruise, the oil pressure gauge drops from the normal 55 PSI to 15 PSI and the oil temperature is beginning to rise. The departure airport is 45 minutes away and the destination is 20 minutes ahead. What is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor the oil pressure for 5 minutes — a brief pressure drop often indicates an oil pressure sensor malfunction rather than actual low oil; if pressure does not recover within 5 minutes, then divert; premature emergency declarations cause disruption and are noted on the pilot's record

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately declare an emergency, reduce power to minimum required for flight, divert to the NEAREST suitable airport (not destination, not departure — the nearest), and prepare for the possibility of engine seizure at any moment; low oil pressure is an engine stoppage emergency; the engine can seize without warning within seconds to minutes of oil pressure loss regardless of how well it seems to be running currently

options.label: C
options.text: Continue to the destination — 20 minutes is shorter than 45 minutes back to departure; reduced oil pressure can be managed by reducing power to 45% and monitoring temperature for the remaining 20 minutes; the engine is still running normally and the destination airport has maintenance facilities

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce power to idle to reduce engine load and conserve the remaining oil; idle power minimizes bearing loads and may allow the aircraft to reach the destination airport before the engine seizes; squawk 7700 after landing to report the event

questions.explanation: Low oil pressure is an engine-seizure emergency — not a monitor-and-continue situation. The mechanism: oil pressure of 15 PSI (with normal being 55 PSI) means the engine's lubrication system is severely compromised. Bearings and journal surfaces depend on an oil film maintained by pressure — below approximately 25 PSI (varies by engine), this film begins to fail. Metal-to-metal contact begins. This generates heat, metal particles, and progressive bearing failure. The engine may appear to run normally for 2-5 minutes after oil pressure is lost — then seize catastrophically with no further warning. 'Only 20 minutes to destination' is the Get-There-Itis rationalization that turns low oil pressure into an in-flight engine seizure at an uncontrolled location. The correct action: NEAREST airport. Not the most convenient. Not the one with maintenance. The nearest. Declare emergency immediately so ATC can vector you directly and have emergency equipment standing by. The 'continue to the destination' answer is the fatal choice — 20 minutes is far beyond the time margin in a low-oil-pressure scenario. The '5-minute monitoring window' answer invents a '5-minute monitoring window' — in an oil pressure emergency, the clock starts now, not after monitoring. A sensor malfunction is a possibility but cannot be confirmed in the aircraft; treat it as real.

questions.text: A pilot lands at a remote airport for fuel. The FBO only stocks 91 octane auto fuel. The pilot's aircraft is certified for 100LL avgas. The FBO agent says: 'Lots of guys use 91 octane here — it works fine, trust me. Your engine won't know the difference on a short hop.' What is the safest decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Accept partial fuel — filling only 40% of the tanks with 91 octane dilutes the impact; mixing 91 octane with any residual 100LL in the tanks brings the effective octane to an acceptable operating range; this is standard practice when mixed fuel grades are the only option at remote airports

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the fuel — aviation engines run cooler and smoother on lower octane fuel; the 100LL requirement is a conservative recommendation; for a short local flight under 30 minutes and below 5,000 feet there is no material difference between 91 octane auto fuel and 100LL avgas

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the fuel but limit power to 55% — at reduced power settings, the compression ratio demand decreases enough that 91 octane auto fuel is within the engine's detonation tolerance; operating at 55% power or less is an accepted mitigation for short hops with lower-octane fuel

options.label: D
options.text: Refuse the fuel — without an FAA-approved STC specifically authorizing auto fuel (mogas) for this aircraft and engine combination, auto fuel is not an approved fuel for this aircraft; using unapproved fuel creates detonation risk due to mismatched octane rating; the correct action is to not accept the fuel, check if the aircraft can safely reach an airport with 100LL, or contact the nearest FBO for aviation fuel delivery

questions.explanation: Using automotive fuel in a piston engine aircraft requires an FAA-issued Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) specifically authorizing that exact aircraft/engine combination for auto fuel use. Without an STC, it is an unapproved modification to the aircraft's type design — regardless of what 'lots of guys' report. The specific hazard: 91 octane auto fuel in an engine certified for 100LL avgas creates detonation risk because the engine's compression ratio was designed around 100-octane fuel's anti-knock characteristics. At high power settings (takeoff, climb), 91 octane may auto-ignite before the timed spark event. The 'partial-fuel and reduced-power mitigation' answers invent mitigation techniques that have no FAA approval: mixing fuel grades does not produce a predictable blended octane in the same way blending paint colors does — fuel chemistry is more complex. Reducing power to 55% may reduce detonation risk but does not make the fuel approved. The proper action: do not accept unapproved fuel, compute whether the aircraft can safely reach an airport with 100LL (accounting for fuel remaining), or contact the regional FBO about fuel delivery to this airport.

questions.text: During the preflight oil check, the oil level reads 4 quarts on the dipstick. The POH states the engine holds 8 quarts maximum and the minimum operating level is 5 quarts. What is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: The oil level is within normal range — 4 quarts in an 8-quart engine is 50% of capacity which is within the acceptable operating window for most aircraft; the minimum oil level of 5 quarts is a cold-start caution, not an in-flight operating minimum

options.label: B
options.text: Fly as planned — 4 quarts is only 1 quart below the minimum; the flight is a short 45-minute local hop; the engine will not experience oil starvation with 4 quarts for 45 minutes

options.label: C
options.text: Drain 1 quart from the engine to bring the level to 3 quarts — the oil system works most efficiently at 3-4 quarts because the reduced oil volume circulates faster, cooling more efficiently per cycle; maximum oil levels cause windage losses from the crankshaft whipping through excess oil

options.label: D
options.text: Add oil to bring the level to at minimum 5 quarts (the POH minimum) before flight; with oil at below minimum level, the aircraft is not airworthy per 14 CFR 91.7; operating below the POH-specified minimum oil level risks oil starvation especially during bank, climb, and high-G maneuvers where oil distribution in the sump becomes uneven

questions.explanation: The POH minimum oil level is a hard airworthiness limit — not an advisory. Operating below 5 quarts when the minimum is 5 quarts makes the aircraft technically non-airworthy under 14 CFR 91.7. The practical risk: at 4 quarts (1 below minimum), oil sump coverage becomes marginal during sustained bank angles, steep descents, or sustained climb attitudes. The oil pickup tube (which draws oil from the sump bottom) can temporarily uncover in steep attitudes — causing a momentary and then sustained drop in oil pressure. This is the direct path to the oil pressure emergency from RKP_04. Additionally, lower oil volume means the oil works harder as a heat-transfer medium — less oil per heat unit generated raises oil temperature and accelerates breakdown. The correct action: add oil before departure to bring the level to at least 5 quarts (minimum) and ideally 6-7 quarts (recommended operating range for most engines). The 'drain down to 3 quarts' answer is dangerously incorrect — draining oil to 3 quarts would be well below minimum and creates immediate risk.

questions.text: A pilot notices during a ground runup that the fuel flow indicator shows intermittently lower-than-normal readings. The fluctuation occurs every 20-30 seconds. The pilot decides to depart since 'the engine is running smoothly.' Under 14 CFR 91.7, is this decision legally and operationally sound?

options.label: A
options.text: No — an intermittent fuel flow anomaly during runup indicates a possible intermittent fuel supply issue (partial blockage, vapor lock, intermittent boost pump spool, or tank vent restriction); smooth current operation does not guarantee continued smooth fuel flow in dynamic flight conditions; 14 CFR 91.7(a) makes the PIC responsible for determining the aircraft is in safe condition; the correct action is to investigate the cause before departure

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — intermittent fuel flow gauge fluctuations are caused by turbulence in the fuel lines during engine vibration and are a routine instrument artifact on piston engines; no fuel system investigation is required; the reading corrects itself once airborne as vibration characteristics change

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — the fuel flow indicator is an advisory instrument only; it is not required for VFR day flight under 14 CFR 91.205; an instrument that is not on the required equipment list can malfunction without making the aircraft unairworthy; smooth engine operation confirms adequate fuel flow regardless of instrument reading

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — the legality and safety depend exclusively on whether the fuel flow gauge is listed in the INOPERATIVE placarding list on the pilot's operating handbook; if the gauge was previously placarded inop by an A&P, it may be legitimately non-functional and the pilot may depart

questions.explanation: An intermittent fuel flow anomaly during runup is a pre-departure warning that demands investigation, not rationalization. The fuel flow gauge (where fitted) reflects actual fuel system pressure and flow — intermittent drops may indicate: (1) Partial blockage in the fuel strainer or fuel lines (debris, water sludge). (2) Intermittent boost pump operation (if boost pump is on). (3) Tank vent restriction causing intermittent vacuum lock. (4) A failing fuel pump (engine-driven or electric). The engine running smoothly during the runup does not guarantee it will continue smoothly during takeoff and climb when fuel demand is highest and the consequences of engine faltering are most severe. 14 CFR 91.7 places the go/no-go determination on the PIC — smooth ground operation does not override an instrument anomaly indicating a potential fuel system defect. The 'fuel flow is advisory only' answer correctly identifies that the fuel flow indicator may not be on the VFR required list — but the issue is not the instrument's airworthiness status; it is what the instrument is INDICATING. Even if the gauge were inoperative (placarded), the intermittent reading would warrant investigation as a potential symptom of a real fuel system issue.

questions.text: On a hot summer day at a high-elevation airport, a pilot departs at full power. During the climb at Vy, the CHT reaches 420°F (above the red line of 400°F). The pilot thinks: 'It's climbing fine — I'll level off at cruise altitude and it'll cool down.' What is the most dangerous element of allowing CHT to exceed the red line?

options.label: A
options.text: Operating above CHT red line creates a direct detonation risk — at 420°F cylinder head temperature, the combustion environment approaches the autoignition conditions for the fuel/air mixture; sustained operation above the red line can cause: detonation, exhaust valve burning, valve seat recession, oil film breakdown on cylinder walls, and piston crown damage; the correct action is to immediately reduce power to bring CHT back to the green arc, or increase airspeed, or open cowl flaps; waiting to level off 'at cruise altitude' delays corrective action when every minute above the red line is causing damage

options.label: B
options.text: The concern is primarily structural — aluminum cylinder heads above 400°F experience accelerated fatigue in the mounting bolt holes; the structural concern is real but develops over hundreds of hours; a single flight above 400°F is not operationally significant

options.label: C
options.text: No danger — the CHT red line represents the temperature at which the engine manufacturer's warranty is voided; operating briefly above the red line does not damage the engine; the 400°F limit has a 15% safety margin built in by the manufacturer

options.label: D
options.text: High CHT in climb is normal and expected — the climb phase always produces the highest CHT due to high power and low ram air cooling; the 400°F limit is the cruise limit, not the climb limit; during normal climbs, CHT may exceed 400°F for up to 10 minutes without concern

questions.explanation: The CHT red line is an operational limit established by the engine manufacturer and reflected in the TCDS and POH — it is not a conservative guideline with a built-in margin. At 420°F CHT: (1) The combustion chamber walls are hotter than normal → the fuel/air charge is pre-warmed above normal → detonation threshold is closer. (2) Exhaust valves operate in the hottest zone of the cylinder → sustained high CHT accelerates valve seat recession and valve face burning → rough running, power loss, eventual valve failure. (3) The oil film on cylinder walls above 400°F approaches the breakdown temperature of mineral aviation oil → increased metal-to-metal contact → premature cylinder wear. Correct immediate corrective actions: (a) Reduce power (reduce manifold pressure or RPM). (b) Enrich the mixture (if leaned — rich mixture provides fuel cooling effect). (c) Increase airspeed (more ram air through the cowl). (d) Open cowl flaps if equipped. 'Wait for cruise altitude' typically takes 3-8 minutes in a climb — at 420°F that is 3-8 minutes of sustained above-limit operation. The 'high CHT is normal in climb' answer is completely false — there is no separate 'climb limit' above the red line. The red line applies in all phases.
questions.sjt_rationale: Complacency and Invulnerability combine to rationalize operating above the red line: 'it's climbing fine' normalizes an instrument indication that is a clear warning. CHT above the red line = act now, not after reaching cruise.

questions.text: A Cessna 172 (high-wing, gravity-feed fuel system) pilot selects BOTH tanks for a cross-country flight. After 90 minutes, the pilot notices the fuel gauge for the RIGHT tank shows nearly empty while the LEFT tank shows over half full. The engine is running normally. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal fuel burn asymmetry — the fuel selector in BOTH position draws more aggressively from the right tank because it is the primary tank; this is expected and the pilot should wait for the left tank to equalize before switching tanks

options.label: B
options.text: A blocked fuel vent on the LEFT tank — if the left tank vent is blocked, atmospheric pressure cannot enter the left tank to replace the fuel volume as fuel is consumed; the resulting partial vacuum prevents fuel from flowing from the left tank; the right tank (with a clear vent) has supplied most of the consumed fuel; the pilot should switch to RIGHT tank only and have the left tank vent inspected on landing

options.label: C
options.text: A stuck or malfunctioning fuel selector — instead of drawing from BOTH tanks equally, the fuel selector is only opening the right side; the selector should be moved to LEFT only immediately to confirm flow from the left tank and equalize tank levels before the right tank empties completely

options.label: D
options.text: Crossfeed from the right to the left tank — in cross-country flight with a right crosswind, fuel migrates from the right tank through the fuel selector to the left tank due to differential pressure from the wing lift asymmetry; this is a known C172 anomaly that requires monitoring but not immediate action

questions.explanation: Asymmetric fuel burn where one tank depletes significantly faster than the other on a 'BOTH' selection is the classic symptom of a blocked tank vent on the fuller tank. Here is the mechanism: the gravity-feed system requires atmospheric pressure to enter each tank (through the fuel tank vent) to replace the fuel volume as fuel drains out. Without this atmospheric equalization, a vacuum develops in the tank, resisting further fuel outflow. The right tank (normal vent) drains normally. The left tank (blocked vent) develops a vacuum and resists draining — its fuel stays in the tank. Over 90 minutes, the right supplies nearly all the consumed fuel. Note: this is not a dangerous emergency yet (engine running normally on right tank fuel), but the right tank is nearly empty. Immediate actions: (1) Switch to LEFT only to verify if fuel flows (if the vent blockage clears, or if the left tank can still provide fuel despite the partial vacuum). (2) Monitor right tank — do not allow it to run dry with only left selected if left tank has a vent blockage. (3) Declare intentions to land soon and have the vent inspected. The 'malfunctioning fuel selector' answer (fuel selector malfunction) is plausible but less likely than vent blockage, and the correction (switch to LEFT) is identical. The 'normal fuel-burn asymmetry' answer invents a 'primary tank' designation for the right side that does not exist in C172 systems.
